a: the division of the days
p: The Ethiopian name of the book, Kufale, is the Ge'ez word for "division" in its first line.
b: The first words call the book an account of the division of the days. The Ge'ez word is kufale, and the Ethiopian churches still call the whole book Kufale. The "division" is a dating system: all of history from creation to Sinai cut into weeks of years and jubilees. The Damascus Document, a rule book of the Dead Sea Scrolls community, sends its readers to the "Book of Time Divisions by Jubilees and Weeks" (column 16, lines 3-4, in E. Cook's translation), which is very likely this book.

a: by their weeks of years and their jubilees
p: Jubilees counts history in weeks of seven years and jubilees of seven weeks, 49 years, not Leviticus's fifty.
b: A "week of years" is seven years, and a jubilee is seven such weeks, 49 years. The book's own arithmetic shows it: Adam dies "at the end of the nineteenth jubilee, in the seventh week, in its sixth year" (4:29), which is 18 × 49 + 6 × 7 + 6 = year 930, the 930 years of Genesis 5:5. Leviticus 25:8-11 makes the jubilee the fiftieth year after seven weeks of years. After the first use the Plain English Translation says "week" where the dating formula repeats.

a: the Lord
p: Ge'ez has no form of God's personal name, so the Plain English Translation writes "the Lord" in small letters.
b: English Bibles print "the LORD" in capitals where the Hebrew has the name YHWH. The Ge'ez of Jubilees has ʾƎgziʾabḥer, "Lord," the word Ethiopian Christians use for God, so this book never shows the divine name. When a note quotes Genesis or Exodus it keeps their "the LORD."

a: on the sixteenth day of the month
p: Exodus 19:1 names only the month. Jubilees supplies the day, the morning after its Feast of Weeks.
b: Exodus says only: "In the third month after the Israelites went out from the land of Egypt, on this same day" (Exodus 19:1). Jubilees dates Moses' climb exactly. Charles 1902 points out how the book uses these dates: the day before, the fifteenth of the third month, is its date for Abraham's feast of the firstfruits (15:1) and for Isaac's birth (16:13), and God speaks to Jacob on the sixteenth (44:5). Goes beyond the Bible: Exodus never ties Sinai to this day.

a: Come up to me on the mountain
p: The book opens inside Exodus 24, at the moment Moses is called up to receive the stone tablets.
b: The words follow Exodus 24:12: "Come up to me on the mountain and stay there. I will give you the stone tablets, with the law and the command that I have written to instruct them." Jubilees adds "two" tablets, a detail Exodus gives later (Exodus 31:18). The whole book is set in the forty days Moses spent on the mountain, so every story in it is heard as part of the revelation at Sinai.

a: a cloud shaded it for six days
p: Verses 2-4 follow Exodus 24:15-18 almost clause by clause.
b: Compare "The glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days" (Exodus 24:16). The seventh-day call (1:3) and the forty days and nights (1:4) follow Exodus 24:16-18. Jubilees hardly changes Exodus here: the new material starts when God begins to speak in 1:5.

a: a blazing fire
p: Exodus 24:17 has a fire that "eats." The Ge'ez has a burning fire; Charles notes how close the two words are.
b: The Ge'ez says the glory looked like a fire "that burns." Exodus 24:17 says the LORD's glory "looked like a fire that eats everything." Charles 1902 notes that a change of one vowel in the Ge'ez would give "devouring," as in Exodus.

a: what came first and what is still to come
p: The book claims that Moses learned on Sinai both the past (Genesis) and the future. The rabbis made a similar claim.
b: Jubilees says God taught Moses the whole past and the whole future on the mountain. Later Jewish teachers said something like it: Charles 1902 quotes the Talmud (Megillah 19b) that God showed Moses "all the minutiae of the law" and what the scribes would later add. The claim gives the book its authority. It is not a later writer's guess about the patriarchs; it presents itself as what Moses was told. Most scholars think the book was written in the 100s BC; see the book's opening pages.

a: write it in a book
p: God tells Moses to write (1:5, 7, 26), then tells the angel of the presence to write for Moses (1:27). Readers have taken this two ways.
b: Moses is told three times to write (1:5, 1:7, 1:26), but in 1:27 God tells the angel of the presence to "write for Moses," and from 2:1 on the angel speaks and Moses writes. Charles 1902 reads 1:26 as Moses writing this book at the angel's dictation, and 1:27 as the angel writing "the book of the first law" (6:22), the five books of Moses. Others read both verses of one book. Either way, Jubilees presents itself as written on Sinai beside the Torah, not after it.

a: For I know how rebellious and stiff-necked they are
p: Verses 7-9 borrow Deuteronomy 31, where God foretells Israel's turning away.
b: Compare Moses' words: "I know your defiance and your stiff neck" (Deuteronomy 31:27). The order of what follows comes from Deuteronomy 31:20: the land of milk and honey, eating their fill, turning to other gods. Jubilees takes the end of Deuteronomy and puts it at the start of the giving of the law, so the whole history is read as God's patience with a people he knew would fail.

a: this testimony will be heard as a witness
p: Like the Song of Moses, the book is meant to stand as evidence against Israel when the troubles come.
b: In Deuteronomy 31:19-26 God gives Moses a song and a book of the law to be a witness against Israel. Jubilees says the same of itself. The word "testimony" runs through the book: the law and the testimony (1:4), the testimony of the heavens (4:30), Enoch's testimony (4:18-19).

a: For they will forget all my commandments
p: From here to the end of the chapter, VanderKam's verse numbers are one higher than Charles's, which most older English books use.
b: The Plain English Translation follows the verse numbers of VanderKam's Ge'ez text. Charles (1902, 1913) counts VanderKam's 1:8 and 1:9 as one verse, 1:8. So VanderKam's 1:10 is Charles's 1:9, and so on to VanderKam's 1:29, which is Charles's 1:28. From chapter 2 on the two numberings agree again.

a: my tent and my sanctuary
p: Charles reads 1:10 as the fall of the northern kingdom and 1:11-13 as the fall of Judah.
b: Charles 1902 sees two disasters here: verse 10 describes the northern tribes, who left the Temple and the feasts and were carried off by Assyria, and verses 11-13 describe Judah's idolatry and exile to Babylon. He notes that if "my tent" belongs to the text, the writer imagined the tabernacle standing in the land during the time of the kings.

a: They will make themselves high places
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez puts "they made" and "they bowed" in the past tense in the middle of a prophecy.
b: Most verbs in God's speech are future, but here VanderKam's Ge'ez has past-tense forms ("they made," "they bowed"); the EOTC copy has future forms. Hebrew and Ge'ez prophecy can speak of a coming event as if already done, and the Plain English Translation keeps the future, with the EOTC copy, so the speech reads as one prophecy. See the variant.

a: They will sacrifice their children to demons
p: The charge comes from Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37, and from the kings who burned their sons.
b: Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37 say Israel sacrificed to demons; 2 Chronicles 28:3 and 33:6 tell of kings who made their sons pass through fire. Jubilees joins the two: the gods of the nations are demons, a view it develops in its story of the spirits after the Flood (10:1-14).

a: They will kill the witnesses
p: The same complaint appears in Nehemiah 9:26 and in Jesus' words in Matthew 23 and Luke 11.
b: "Witnesses" are the prophets. Nehemiah 9:26 and 2 Chronicles 24:19 say Israel killed or ignored the prophets God sent. Jesus makes the same charge (Matthew 23:34-37; Luke 11:47-51), and Charles 1902 lists Luke 11:49 beside this verse. Agrees with the Bible's own account of the prophets.

a: They will go wrong about the start of the month and about Sabbaths, feasts, jubilees and ordinances
t: The calendar as the great sin
p: In this book, forgetting the right days is as serious as idolatry. It is the first sign of the calendar quarrel behind Jubilees.
b: The exiles' sin is not only bowing to idols but keeping the first days of the months, the Sabbaths and the feasts on the wrong days. Jubilees argues for a year of 364 days, with feasts that always fall on the same day of the week (see 6:23-38), and against reckoning by the moon. Historical critics read this verse as a sign that the writer's real opponents were other Jews who kept a different calendar in his own day.

a: the start of the month
t: "The start of the month," not "new moon"
p: Charles's English has "new moons." The Ge'ez word is the one Jubilees uses for the first day of a month.
b: The Ge'ez śärq is the book's word for the first day of a month (3:32; 6:23). Charles's English (1913) has "new moons," and many translations follow him. But Jubilees does not let the moon set its months: the sun alone is the sign for days, months and feasts (2:9), and 6:36-38 condemns counting by the moon. So the Plain English Translation says "the start of the month" in this list and "the first day" in dates.

a: I will let them find me
p: The promise follows Jeremiah 29:13-14 and Deuteronomy 4:29.
b: After the exile they will seek God with all their heart, and he will be found, as Jeremiah 29:13-14 and Deuteronomy 4:29-31 promise. Jubilees sets these promises in Moses' own hearing, so the return from exile becomes part of what Sinai already foresaw.

a: I will transplant them as a plant of uprightness
p: Israel as God's planting. Charles thought the Ge'ez here was damaged and that Jeremiah 32:41 lies behind it.
b: The Ge'ez verb means "move" or "transplant." Charles 1902 marked the phrase as corrupt and suggested the original said "I will plant them," as in Jeremiah 32:41, which goes on, "with all my heart and all my being," close to the words that follow here. The picture of the righteous as a plant is common in this literature: 1 Enoch speaks of "the plant of righteousness and truth" (1 Enoch 10:16).

a: They will be the head and not the tail
p: From the blessings of Deuteronomy 28:13; "a blessing and not a curse" comes from Zechariah 8:13.
b: Deuteronomy 28:13 promises that an obedient Israel will be the head and not the tail. Zechariah 8:13 promises that the people who were a curse among the nations will become a blessing. Jubilees weaves both into God's promise to Moses.

a: I will build my sanctuary among them and live with them
p: The covenant formula of the Torah and the prophets, which Revelation 21:3 also uses.
b: Compare "I will live among the Israelites, and I will be their God" (Exodus 29:45), and Leviticus 26:11-12, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 37:26-27. Charles 1902 takes the sanctuary here as the Second Temple built after the return. Paul quotes the formula in 2 Corinthians 6:16, and Revelation 21:3 places its fulfillment in the new Jerusalem.
r: Exodus 25:8; Exodus 29:45; Leviticus 26:11-12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:26-27; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:3

a: Moses fell on his face and prayed
p: The prayer echoes Moses' plea in Deuteronomy 9:26-29 for God's people and inheritance.
b: In Deuteronomy 9:26-29 Moses prays that God will not destroy "your people, your inheritance," whom he brought out of Egypt. Jubilees gives Moses a new prayer with the same words (1:19, 21), but its request is inward: a new spirit and freedom from the spirit of Beliar.

a: the spirit of Beliar
p: Beliar is a name for the leader of evil spirits, the same name Paul uses in 2 Corinthians 6:15.
b: Moses asks that "the spirit of Beliar" not rule Israel or accuse them before God. Paul uses the same name: "How can Christ be in tune with Beliar?" (2 Corinthians 6:15). In Jubilees the evil spirits have a chief, called Mastema in the later chapters (10:8), and Beliar appears again in 15:33.

a: to accuse them before you
p: The evil spirit's work is to accuse God's people before him, as in Job, Zechariah and Revelation.
b: In Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1 an accuser stands before God against his servants; in Revelation 12:10 the accuser of our brothers is thrown down. Agrees with this picture. Goes beyond: Moses' prayer treats the accuser as a spirit that can rule a people and lead them away from righteousness.

a: Create a clean heart and a holy spirit in them
p: The words come from Psalm 51:10-11.
b: Psalm 51:10-11 asks God to create a clean heart and not to take away his holy spirit. Jubilees puts the psalm's prayer on Moses' lips for the whole nation. God's answer in 1:23 promises exactly this.

a: until they confess their own sin and the sin of their fathers
p: Leviticus 26:40 sets the same condition for return: confessing their sin and their fathers' sin.
b: Leviticus 26:40-42 promises that God will remember his covenant when the exiles confess their sins and their ancestors'. Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9 show such prayers being prayed after the exile.

a: I will circumcise the foreskin of their hearts
p: Deuteronomy, Jeremiah and Ezekiel promise a changed heart. Paul says true circumcision is of the heart.
b: Compare "The LORD your God will circumcise your heart, and your descendants' hearts too" (Deuteronomy 30:6), with Deuteronomy 10:16, Jeremiah 4:4 and Ezekiel 36:26-27. Paul writes that "circumcision is of the heart, in spirit and not in letter" (Romans 2:29). Agrees with these promises. Differs in use: Jubilees insists elsewhere on bodily circumcision on the eighth day (15:25-34), so for it the inner change is added to the outward sign, not put in its place; Paul argues that for Gentiles in Christ the sign is not required.

a: I will be their father, and they will be my children
p: The promise to David's son (2 Samuel 7:14) becomes a promise to all Israel. Paul gives it to the church.
b: Charles 1902 notes that "I will be his father" is said of Solomon in 2 Samuel 7:14, and that the Old Testament elsewhere calls Israel God's son (Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1). Here all Israelites are God's children by descent from Jacob. Paul applies the words to believers (2 Corinthians 6:18). Matches the Old Testament idea; the New Testament widens the family.

a: children of the living God
p: The title comes from Hosea 1:10, which Paul quotes in Romans 9:26.
b: Hosea 1:10 promises that those called "not my people" will be called children of the living God. Jubilees uses the title for restored Israel; Paul quotes Hosea for Jews and Gentiles called in Christ (Romans 9:24-26).

a: until I come down and live with them for all ages to come
t: God comes down to live with them
p: The book looks ahead to God's own dwelling with his people, the hope of Ezekiel and Revelation.
b: Charles 1902 reads this as the writer's view of history: from creation to the day God himself lives among his people. Ezekiel 43:7 and Zechariah 2:10-11 promise it; Revelation 21:3 says "God's tent is with human beings." Jubilees ties that end to Zion and the sanctuary (1:27-29; 4:26).

a: the angel of the presence
p: Literally "the angel of the face," one of the highest angels. He narrates the rest of the book.
b: The Ge'ez means "angel of the face," an angel who stands before God's face. The phrase comes from Isaiah 63:9, "the angel of his presence saved them." Charles 1902 thinks this is probably Michael, Israel's guardian angel in Daniel 10:21 and 12:1, but the book never names him. From 2:1 on he speaks to Moses, and his "we" means the angels of the presence (2:18).

a: Write for Moses
p: Exodus says God wrote the tablets. Jubilees has an angel write for Moses, an idea the New Testament also knows.
b: In Exodus the stone tablets are "written by God's own finger" (Exodus 31:18). Here an angel writes for Moses. Charles 1902 calls this the earliest witness to the idea that the law came through angels. Stephen says, "You were given the law by the orders of angels" (Acts 7:53); Paul, "It was arranged through angels, by the hand of a mediator" (Galatians 3:19); Hebrews 2:2 speaks of "the word spoken through angels." Goes beyond Exodus, but agrees with a belief the New Testament treats as known. Paul uses it to rank the law below the promise.

a: King on Mount Zion
p: Isaiah 24:23 pictures the LORD reigning on Mount Zion. Charles thought this verse once stood after 1:25.
b: Isaiah 24:23 says the LORD will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem. Here God is the father of Jacob's children and King on Zion. Charles 1902 notes that the verse breaks the line of thought and probably belonged after 1:25. Compare Revelation 1:7, where every eye will see him.

a: who goes in front of the camps of Israel
t: The angel who went before the camp
p: The angel of the presence is the angel of the Exodus.
b: The phrase comes from Exodus 14:19: "The angel of God, who had been going ahead of Israel's camp." Jubilees identifies the angel who led Israel through the sea with the angel who now dictates the book.

a: the tablets of the division of the years
p: Besides Moses' stone tablets, the angel holds tablets of the years, from which he reads the dates of history.
b: The Ge'ez here says "the tablets of the division of the years," using the word kufale again (see 1:0). They are not the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments but heavenly tablets of dates, from which the angel dictates. From 3:10 on the book speaks of "the heavenly tablets," where laws and events are written in heaven.

a: the heavens and the earth and all their creatures will be renewed
p: Jubilees expects a new creation centered on Zion. Charles thought it pictured a gradual change, not a sudden end.
b: Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth; 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1 look for them. Charles 1902 argues that Jubilees pictures a slow renewal, moving step by step with Israel's return to the law (compare 23:26-29), rather than a sudden end. Other readers hear a final new creation like Revelation's.

a: All the lights will be renewed for healing
p: The sun, moon and stars made new. Charles compares the leaves for healing in Revelation 22:2.
b: The "lights" are the sun, moon and stars. Their renewal fits the book's concern with the calendar: in the new creation the lights will keep perfect time. Charles 1902 compares the leaves "for healing the nations" in Revelation 22:2.

a: Write the whole account of creation
p: Chapter 2 retells Genesis 1:1-2:3 day by day, counting the works and ending with the Sabbath.
b: The angel now begins: creation (2:1-16) and the Sabbath (2:17-33) follow Genesis 1:1-2:3. Charles 1902 quotes a Greek note on Exodus 24:15 in a Paris manuscript (Coislin) that knows this tradition: after the forty days Moses saw in visions how God made the heavens and the earth in six days, and was told to write it down.

a: all the spirits who serve before him
t: Angels made on the first day
p: Genesis does not say when the angels were made. Jubilees puts them on day one; some rabbis said the second or fifth day.
b: Genesis 1 never mentions angels. Jubilees counts them among the seven works of the first day. Charles 1902 reports that rabbis in Genesis Rabbah put the angels on the second day (Rabbi Yohanan) or the fifth (Rabbi Hanina), and one said they were not made on day one so no one could say they helped God create. Job 38:7 has the sons of God shouting for joy at the founding of the earth. Goes beyond the Bible, but no verse of the 66 contradicts it; Colossians 1:16 says all things in heaven, visible and invisible, were created through Christ.

a: the angels of the spirit of fire
p: A lower rank of angels runs fire, wind, cloud, weather and seasons, as in Revelation 7 and 16.
b: Below the angels of the presence and of holiness come angels in charge of nature. Revelation knows the same idea: four angels hold back the four winds (Revelation 7:1), an angel has power over fire (Revelation 14:18), and "the angel of the waters" speaks (Revelation 16:5). Charles 1902 also points to 1 Enoch 60:11-21. In Jubilees these lower angels are not said to keep the Sabbath (2:18).

a: the angels of the voices, of the thunders and of the lightnings
p: The same three words come together in Revelation 4:5, 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18.
b: Charles 1902 notes that Revelation joins the same three, lightnings, voices and thunders (Revelation 4:5), and similar lists, and suggests the "voices" are the rumbling of thunder, as in Job 37:4.

a: he made seven great works on the first day
p: Jubilees counts 22 works of creation: 7, 1, 4, 3, 3 and 4 over the six days.
b: The angel numbers the works: seven on the first day (heavens, earth, waters, spirits, the depths, darkness, light and its times), one on the second (2:4), four on the third (2:7), three on the fourth (2:10), three on the fifth (2:12), four on the sixth (2:14), twenty-two in all (2:15). Charles 1902 shows that a later Hebrew work, Midrash Tadshe, counts the same twenty-two and also links them to the twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob (see 2:23). How the first day's seven are counted depends on whether "the depths" is a separate work; the Greek of Epiphanius makes it one.

a: the dome
p: The same word as Genesis 1:6, which the site renders "dome": the solid vault above the sky.
b: The Ge'ez məṣnaʿat means something made firm, like the Greek stereōma and the Hebrew raqia of Genesis 1:6. The Plain English Translation uses "dome," as the site's Genesis does. Older English Bibles say "firmament."

a: for delight and for all
p: The Ge'ez words after "the garden of Eden" look damaged. Charles supplied "plants after their kind" from the Greek.
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez reads "the garden of Eden in Eden, for delight and for all," and the Plain English Translation renders it word for word. Charles 1902 judged the words damaged: "for delight" is either a second translation of "in Eden" (the Hebrew name means delight) or a corruption of the Ge'ez word for "plants"; "in Eden" is also extra. His English, "and all plants after their kind," comes from the Greek of Epiphanius, which ends the list of the third day's works with "all the plants according to their kind." See the variant.

a: the garden of Eden
t: Eden made on the third day
p: Genesis 2:8 does not date the planting of the garden. Jubilees puts it on the third day with the other plants.
b: Genesis 2:8 says the LORD God planted a garden in Eden but gives no day. Jubilees, which lets nothing go undated, sets it among the plants of the third day. Goes beyond Genesis, filling a gap rather than changing it.

a: The Lord made the sun a great sign
t: The sun alone sets the times
p: Genesis 1:14 makes both lights signs for seasons. Jubilees gives the job to the sun alone.
b: Genesis 1:14 says of the lights together: "They will be signs, and will mark the appointed times, the days and the years." Jubilees quietly leaves the moon out: only the sun marks days, Sabbaths, months, feasts, years and jubilees. This prepares for the book's argument for a 364-day solar year and against counting by the moon (6:23-38). Narrows Genesis. The later Jewish calendar reckons its months by the moon.

a: for these were the first creatures of flesh made by his hands
p: The sea creatures come first among living things, as in Genesis 1:20-23.
b: Genesis 1:21 says God "created the great sea monsters" on the fifth day, the first time since 1:1 that Genesis uses the verb "create." Jubilees explains the order: these were the first creatures of flesh. Its four kinds on the sixth day end with humankind (2:14).

a: he made one human being: he made them a man and a woman
p: From Genesis 1:27. Jubilees leaves out "in our image" and "in God's image."
b: Genesis 1:26-27 says God made humankind in his image, male and female. Jubilees keeps "man and woman" and the rule over the creatures (Genesis 1:28), but says nothing here of God's image. In chapter 3 it retells the second creation account of Genesis 2.

a: twenty-two kinds
p: The number is the key to 2:23: twenty-two works, twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob.
b: The total of twenty-two (see 2:3) matters to the writer because Jacob, the father of Israel, is the twenty-second head of humankind from Adam (2:23). The number of the Hebrew letters is twenty-two as well, and Greek Christian writers who used Jubilees made that link (see the variant at 2:23).

a: He gave us a great sign, the Sabbath day
p: Exodus 31:13 calls the Sabbath a sign between God and Israel. Here it is first a sign among the angels.
b: Compare "For this is a sign between me and you through your generations" (Exodus 31:13). In Jubilees the Sabbath is a sign before Israel exists: God gives it to the highest angels, who keep it with him (2:18). Agrees that the Sabbath is a sign; goes beyond Exodus in making it a heavenly law from creation. On how churches differ about the Sabbath, see the "Where Christians differ" cards on Exodus 16-24 and Colossians 2.

a: to keep Sabbath with him in heaven and on earth
p: Only the two highest ranks of angels keep Sabbath with God. The angels over nature keep working.
b: Charles 1902 notes that only the angels of the presence and of holiness keep the Sabbath; the angels of wind and weather must keep working (2:2). Israel will join the highest angels (2:21, 28). Genesis 2:2-3 says God rested; Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for God's people. Goes beyond the Bible: no verse of the 66 says angels keep the Sabbath.

a: I will set apart a people for myself
p: The language of 1 Kings 8:53 and Leviticus 20:26, said on the first Sabbath of creation.
b: Leviticus 20:26 and 1 Kings 8:53 speak of God setting Israel apart from the peoples. In Jubilees God says it to the angels in the first week of the world, before any human exists. Israel's election is as old as creation.

a: my firstborn son
p: From Exodus 4:22, "Israel is my son, my firstborn."
b: Moses is to tell Pharaoh, "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22). Jubilees says God already wrote Jacob down as his firstborn in the first week. The phrase "written down" fits the book's heavenly records (see 3:10).

a: to eat and drink and bless the one who created everything
p: The Sabbath in Jubilees is a feast: eating, drinking and blessing God. Fasting on it is forbidden later (50:12).
b: Charles 1902 points out that the book stresses the joy of the Sabbath again in 2:31 and 50:9-10, and forbids fasting on it in 50:12. Jewish practice also treats the Sabbath as a day of good meals and blessing (Isaiah 58:13 calls it "a delight"). Jesus says the Sabbath was made for humankind (Mark 2:27).

a: a pleasing fragrance
p: The language of sacrifice (Genesis 8:21) used for keeping God's commands.
b: "Pleasing fragrance" is the phrase for an acceptable sacrifice (Genesis 8:21; Exodus 29:18). Paul uses it of Christ's self-giving (Ephesians 5:2). Charles 1902 judged the beginning of this verse corrupt, and the end of it breaks off: see the variant at 2:23.

a: his desires
p: Charles marked this verse corrupt and rendered the noun "His commands." Its sense is uncertain.
b: The Ge'ez says, word for word, "and he made his fäqadat rise as a pleasing fragrance." Charles 1902 rendered the noun "His commands" and marked the words "Corrupt." The Plain English Translation gives the plain sense of the Ge'ez, "his desires" (that is, what God wills), but the verse is probably damaged, and its end breaks off (see the variant at 2:23).

a: from Adam down to him
p: "Him" is Jacob. From Adam to Jacob there are twenty-two generations, as there are twenty-two works.
b: Counting by the lists of Genesis 5 and 11, without Kainam (whom the Greek Genesis and 8:1-5 add), Jacob is the twenty-second head of humankind. Charles 1902 explains the pairing: as the Sabbath comes at the close of the twenty-two works, so Jacob comes at the close of the twenty-two generations, and only with Jacob could the Sabbath be kept rightly on earth. "This one" is the Sabbath and "that one" is Jacob.

a: anyone who does any work on it is to die
p: The penalty of Exodus 31:14-15, here declared at creation.
b: Exodus 31:15 says: "Anyone who does work on the Sabbath day must be put to death." Numbers 15:32-36 tells of a man stoned for gathering wood. Matches the Torah's penalty. Goes beyond it in 2:27, where the one who works "must surely die forever." Jesus' disputes about the Sabbath (Mark 2:23-3:6) show that Jews of his day argued about what counted as work; this book takes the strictest side (50:6-13).

a: or draw water, or carry in through their gates any load
p: Carrying loads through the gates is forbidden as in Jeremiah 17:21-22 and Nehemiah 13:19; drawing water is added.
b: Jeremiah 17:21-22 forbids carrying a load through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath, and Nehemiah 13:19 shuts the gates against it. John 5:10 shows the same rule in Jesus' time. Charles 1902 compares the Mishnah's rule against carrying from one domain to another (Shabbat 7:2), and thinks the clauses of this verse have been disordered in copying. Food for the Sabbath must be prepared the day before, as with the manna (Exodus 16:23).

a: We kept Sabbath on it in the heavens
p: The angels kept the Sabbath before any human did.
b: For Jubilees the feasts and the Sabbath are heavenly before they are earthly; Charles 1902 notes that the Feast of Weeks too was kept in heaven until Noah (6:18). No verse of the 66 says so. Goes beyond the Bible.

a: only Israel
p: Jubilees says the Sabbath was given to Israel alone, not to the nations.
b: Exodus 31:16-17 and Ezekiel 20:12 call the Sabbath a sign between God and Israel. Jubilees presses the point: God did not make the nations holy to keep it. Agrees with the Torah that the Sabbath is Israel's covenant sign. Christians read the matter in different ways: for the main positions see the "Where Christians differ" cards on the Sabbath (Exodus 16-24; Colossians 2:16-17).

a: The Creator of all gave his blessing
p: The Ge'ez has no object. Charles changed one vowel to read "blessed it," meaning Israel.
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez says only "and the Creator of all blessed." Charles 1902 notes that the manuscripts lack "it" and, following Barth and Littmann, changed the verb's last vowel to read "blessed her," which he took as Israel. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez as it stands.

a: as a law forever, for their generations
p: The phrase of the priestly laws in Exodus and Leviticus.
b: Charles 1902 notes that this is the Hebrew ḥuqqat ʿolam ledorotam, "a lasting rule for their generations" (Exodus 27:21; Leviticus 23:14). For Jubilees the laws it teaches are eternal. Christian readers set this beside Hebrews 7-8, where parts of the law are said to be changed.

a: During the six days of the second week
p: Jubilees spreads Genesis 2 over the second week of creation: the animals named on days 8 to 12.
b: Genesis 2:19-20 tells how the animals were brought to the man, with no dates. Jubilees gives each kind its own day. Charles 1902 quotes Syncellus, a Greek chronicler of about AD 800, who knew this scheme: on the first day Adam named the wild animals, on the second the herd animals, then the birds, the creeping things and the swimming things.

a: we brought to Adam
p: In Genesis God brings the animals to the man. In Jubilees the angels do it at God's word.
b: Genesis 2:19 says the LORD God "brought them to the man." Here the angels bring them, and later they bring Adam and Eve into the garden (3:9, 12) and teach Adam to farm (3:15). Goes beyond Genesis: the book keeps God at a distance and gives his acts to his angels.

a: Let us make him a helper
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 2:18 says "I will make." Jubilees agrees with the Greek and Latin "let us make."
b: Genesis 2:18 in the Hebrew reads "I will make him a helper who is his match." Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees' "let us make" agrees with the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus) and the Vulgate (Jerome's Latin). In Jubilees God speaks to the angels: "The Lord said to us."

a: this rib was what the woman was created from
p: The Ge'ez says "one bone from among his bones" and then calls it a rib or side.
b: Charles 1902 notes that the Ge'ez literally says "one bone from among his bones," and then "this rib (or side)." The Hebrew word in Genesis 2:21, tsela, also means "side."

a: he got up on the sixth day
p: The sixth day of the second week: the woman is made on the thirteenth day of the world.
b: Charles 1902 counts this as the thirteenth day of creation. Jubilees separates Genesis 1:27 ("male and female," day six of the first week, 2:14) from Genesis 2:21-22 (the woman built from the rib) by a week. That gap becomes the reason for the law of 3:8-11.

a: This one will be called my wife, because she was taken from her husband
p: Genesis 2:23 plays on Hebrew ish (man) and ishah (woman). The Ge'ez cannot, and says "my wife."
b: The site's Genesis 2:23 reads: "This one will be called Woman, because from Man this one was taken." The Hebrew ishah sounds like ish. Ge'ez has no such pair, so it says "my wife" and "her husband." Charles 1902 notes that "my" is also in the Ethiopic Genesis, and "her husband" agrees with the Samaritan text, the Septuagint and the Targum of Onkelos.

a: they become one flesh
p: Genesis 2:24 word for word. Jubilees does not have "the two," which Jesus' quotation has.
b: The site's Genesis 2:24 reads, "So a man leaves his father and his mother and sticks close to his wife, and they become one flesh." Jesus quotes it with "the two will become one flesh" (Matthew 19:5), as the Septuagint has it. Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees agrees with the Hebrew in lacking "the two."

a: That is why the command was given
t: Why the purity law has these numbers
p: Leviticus 12 sets 40 days after a boy's birth and 80 after a girl's. Jubilees finds the reason in Eden.
b: Leviticus 12:2-5 gives the numbers: seven plus thirty-three days for a boy, fourteen plus sixty-six for a girl. Leviticus gives no reason. Jubilees says Adam entered Eden after forty days and Eve after eighty (3:9). Charles 1902 shows that Syncellus and Glycas knew this, and that Midrash Tadshe gives the same reason in the name of Pinchas ben Jair, though Beer found no trace of it elsewhere in rabbinic literature. Goes beyond the Bible: it gives a law of Moses a reason from the first week of the world. Luke 2:22-24 shows Mary keeping this law after Jesus' birth.

a: His wife they brought in
p: The verb changes from "we" to "they." The Ge'ez often uses "they" for an act whose doer is not named.
b: Adam is brought in by "us," the angels, but Eve by "they." Ge'ez often uses a plain "they" to mean "she was brought," and 3:12 has "we brought her" again.

a: the heavenly tablets
p: The book's first mention of laws written in heaven. Its Ge'ez word differs from 1 Enoch's, but the idea is the same.
b: The Ge'ez ṣəlatä sämay means "tablets of heaven." 1 Enoch speaks of the same thing with another word, ṣäfṣäfä sämay (1 Enoch 81:1-2; 93:2), and the site renders both "the heavenly tablets." Charles 1902 describes how Jubilees uses the idea in three ways: the heavenly law book, of which the law of Moses is the copy on earth; a record of events as they happen; and a book of what is to come.

a: She must not touch anything holy or come into the sanctuary
p: The wording of the law matches Leviticus 12:4.
b: Compare "She must not touch anything holy or come into the sanctuary until her days of purifying are over" (Leviticus 12:4). The "blood of her purifying" is the bleeding after birth. The law is about ritual purity before entering God's sanctuary, not about moral guilt.

a: for it is holier than all the earth
p: Eden is treated like the Temple: holy ground that may not be entered while impure.
b: Because Eden is holy, Adam and Eve enter it only after the days of purity, as a mother later enters the sanctuary. Eden is one of the Lord's four holy places (4:26). Ezekiel 28:13-14 places Eden on "the holy mountain of God," and Adam's work in Genesis 2:15, "to work it and to guard it," uses the two Hebrew verbs ('avad, shamar) that Numbers 3:7-8 uses for the Levites' duties at the tabernacle.

a: seven years
p: Jubilees gives Adam seven years in Eden. Some rabbis gave him only hours.
b: Charles 1902 notes that Genesis Rabbah 18, the Talmud (Sanhedrin 38b) and the Syriac Cave of Treasures say Adam was in the garden only six hours. Jubilees, which sets the Fall in the second month of the eighth year (3:17), gives him seven years of work. Genesis itself does not say how long.

a: He put away what was being kept
p: The last clause seems to repeat the one before it. Charles thought a copyist doubled it.
b: Charles 1902 bracketed the clause as a dittography, a phrase copied twice by mistake, and explained how a Hebrew word for "what was left" could have been misread as "what was kept." The Plain English Translation keeps it, since it is in VanderKam's text.

a: in the second month, on the seventeenth day
p: The Fall comes on the 17th of the second month. The couple leave Eden on the 1st of the fourth (3:32).
b: Charles 1902 notes that Syncellus, quoting "the Little Genesis," says they were cast out forty-five days after the sin, which fits these two dates. The same date, the second month and seventeenth day, is the day the Flood began in Genesis 7:11.

a: the snake
p: The Ge'ez word for the snake means "beast of the earth."
b: The Ge'ez calls the tempter ʾärwe mədr, literally "beast of the earth," the usual Ge'ez word for a snake. Jubilees, like Genesis, does not call it Satan. Later readers did: Revelation 12:9 calls the great dragon "the ancient snake, the one called the devil and Satan."

a: you will be like gods
p: The Ge'ez has a plural, "gods." The Hebrew elohim can mean God or gods; the site's Genesis says "like God."
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 3:5 has elohim, which can be read as "God" or "gods" (or "divine beings"). The site's Genesis renders it "like God." The Ge'ez here has the plural ʾämalkət, "gods," like the Greek and the KJV's "as gods."

a: She first covered her nakedness with fig leaves
p: In Genesis both see their nakedness after both have eaten. Here Eve covers herself before she gives the fruit to Adam.
b: Genesis 3:7 says the eyes of the two of them were opened after both ate. Jubilees has Eve cover herself first, then Adam. Goes beyond Genesis. The change fits the book's concern with covering nakedness (3:22, 27, 30-31).

a: was angry with it forever
t: Did the snake lose its feet?
p: Charles thought something was lost here: Greek writers say Jubilees told how the snake lost its feet.
b: Charles 1902 marked a gap after this clause. He points out that the Greek chronicler Glycas says the book taught that the snake once had hands and feet, taken away because it entered Paradise, and that Syncellus says it had four feet. He also quotes the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 3:14, "your feet will be cut off," and Josephus (Antiquities 1.1.4), who says God took away the snake's voice and feet. VanderKam's Ge'ez has no gap here; it runs straight on to the woman's sentence.

a: Your return will be to your husband
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 3:16 has "desire." Jubilees agrees with the Greek "your turning" or "return."
b: The site's Genesis 3:16 reads "Your desire will be for your husband," from the Hebrew teshuqah. Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees here matches the Greek apostrophē, "turning," found in the Septuagint and the Syriac, which read a Hebrew word for "return" (teshuvah).

a: your sorrow and your pain
p: The Hebrew has "your pain and your pregnancies." Jubilees agrees with the Greek.
b: The site's Genesis 3:16 reads "I will make your pain and your pregnancies very great." Charles 1902 notes that "your pains" for "your pregnancies" agrees with the Septuagint.

a: he burned incense as a pleasing fragrance
p: Adam offers the incense that Exodus 30:34 reserves for the sanctuary.
b: Exodus 30:34 lists the spices of the sanctuary incense: "Take spices: stacte, onycha and galbanum, spices mixed with pure frankincense." Jubilees has Adam burn such incense as he leaves Eden. Charles 1902 notes that the writer moves the incense offering back to Adam, and that the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 8a) says Adam offered an ox. Goes beyond the Bible: Genesis records no offering by Adam. Jubilees makes the patriarchs priests long before Aaron (compare Enoch in 4:25).

a: once he had covered his nakedness
p: A priest must not be exposed at the altar (Exodus 20:26; 28:42).
b: Charles 1902 notes, following Beer, that Exodus 20:26 and 28:42 may lie behind this: priests must not expose themselves at the altar, so Adam offers only after he is clothed.

a: frankincense, galbanum, stacte and spices
p: The four Ge'ez spice names are rare words. The English names follow Charles.
b: After the word for incense the Ge'ez names four ingredients: səḥin, qənʾät, mayä ləbn and sänbält. These are rare words, and the Plain English Translation names them as Charles's English (1913) does: frankincense, galbanum, stacte and spices. Exodus 30:34 lists stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense for the sanctuary incense.
orig: ስሒነ ፡ ወቅንአተ ፡ ወማየ ፡ ልብን ፡ ወሰንበልተ (səḥinä wäqnəʾätä wämayä ləbn wäsänbältä)

a: so that they could not speak
p: Jubilees says all animals spoke until the expulsion. Josephus says the same.
b: Genesis has a talking snake (Genesis 3:1) and later a talking donkey (Numbers 22:28), but says nothing about animals in general. Charles 1902 quotes Josephus (Antiquities 1.1.4), "all animals were of the same language at that time," and Syncellus, who names Josephus and "the Little Genesis" together for it. The book later calls the first language Hebrew, "the language of creation" (12:25-26). Verdict: a Jewish tradition shared by Jubilees and Josephus, not a borrowing from other peoples' myths.

a: one speech and one language
p: The phrase of Genesis 11:1, used of the animals before the Fall.
b: Compare "The whole earth had one language and one set of words" (Genesis 11:1). Jubilees uses the words of the Babel story for the speech of all creatures in Eden.

a: not uncover themselves as the nations uncover themselves
p: Charles read this as a protest against Jews who exercised naked in the Greek gymnasium in Jerusalem.
b: Charles 1902 called this verse of great historical importance: a protest against the Greek custom of exercising naked, brought into Jerusalem when a gymnasium was built there under the high priest Jason (1 Maccabees 1:14-15; 2 Maccabees 4:9-14). The writer finds the reason in Genesis 3:21: God clothed Adam, and only Adam. Here the Ge'ez says "on the tablets" without "heavenly"; Charles's text has "the heavenly tablets."

a: the land of Elda
p: A place name found only here. Charles wondered whether it hides a Hebrew word for "birthplace."
b: Genesis 3:23 says Adam was sent to work the ground "he had been taken from." Jubilees names it Elda, "the land where they were created." Charles 1902 asked whether Elda could be a corruption of Hebrew moledet, "birthplace," and notes that the Targums of Genesis 3:23 also say "where he was created."

a: On the first day of the fourth month
p: Charles's English has "new moon"; Jubilees does not let the moon set its months.
b: The Ge'ez śärq marks the first day of a month, as in 1:14. Charles's English has "on the new moon of the fourth month," but this book makes the sun alone the sign for months and feasts (2:9). Charles 1902 adds that Syncellus gives Adam forty-five days in the garden after his sin, which fits this text: he sinned on the 17th of the second month (3:17) and left on the 1st of the fourth.

a: They had no son until the first jubilee
p: Jubilees puts Cain's birth after the first jubilee, outside the garden, as Genesis 4:1 implies.
b: Charles 1902 notes that the Syriac Cave of Treasures says Adam and Eve left Paradise as virgins. Genesis 4:1 tells of Cain's birth after the expulsion. Agrees with Genesis, and adds the date.

a: In the third week of the second jubilee
p: The third week of the second jubilee is the years 64 to 70 from creation.
b: One jubilee (49 years) plus two weeks (14) brings the count to year 63, so the third week of the second jubilee is the years 64-70. Charles 1902 notes that Syncellus puts Cain's birth in year 70 and Awan's in 85, dates he says were drawn from this book.

a: his daughter Awan
p: Genesis names no daughters of Adam. Jubilees names two: Awan, Cain's wife, and Azura, Seth's (4:8).
b: The Ge'ez name is ʾAwan. Charles 1902 lists other forms of the two sisters' names: in the Syriac list of the patriarchs' wives Aswa and Azura; in Epiphanius Saue and Azoura; in Syncellus Asaunan and Azoura. He suggested Awan comes from Hebrew 'awen, "wickedness." The book answers an old question, where Cain's wife came from (Genesis 4:17): she was his sister.

a: Abel's offering
p: Genesis 4:4-5 gives no reason. Hebrews says Abel offered by faith.
b: Genesis 4:4-5 says only that the LORD looked kindly at Abel's gift and not at Cain's. "By faith Abel offered God a fuller sacrifice than Cain's" (Hebrews 11:4); 1 John 3:12 says Cain's deeds were evil. On the text of this verse, see the next note.

a: because God accepted Abel's offering
p: The Plain English Translation follows Dillmann's Ge'ez; Charles's English has the two words the other way round.
b: The Ge'ez text this site uses is damaged in this verse as transcribed, and the verse is translated from Dillmann's edition (1859): God accepted from Abel's hand an offering (qʷərban) and did not accept Cain's sacrifice (məśwaʿt). Charles's English has "accepted the sacrifice of Abel, and did not accept the offering of Cain." His note shows that the manuscripts differ in wording: for Abel, manuscript a has "the sacrifice of Abel" and b, c, d "the sacrifice at his hand"; the word "offering" stands in a and c and is missing in b and d; for Cain, a has "of Cain" and b, c, d "at the hand of Cain." The sense is the same.

a: his blood cried out from the ground to heaven
p: Genesis 4:10; the same image appears in 1 Enoch 22 and Hebrews 12:24.
b: Compare "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Charles 1902 compares 1 Enoch 22:5-7, where Abel's spirit keeps accusing Cain's descendants. Hebrews 12:24 speaks of the blood of sprinkling "which speaks better than Abel."

a: a wanderer
t: A Hebrew word in Ge'ez letters
p: The Ge'ez word here is not Ge'ez: Charles saw in it the Hebrew na', "wanderer," of Genesis 4:12.
b: Charles 1902 explains the Ge'ez nuḫ as a corrupt spelling of the Hebrew word of Genesis 4:12, where Cain is to be "a homeless wanderer" (na' wanad). A Hebrew word carried through Greek into Ge'ez is one sign that the book was first written in Hebrew.

a: Cursed is anyone who strikes his neighbor by treachery
t: A law of Deuteronomy in Cain's story
p: The curse of Deuteronomy 27:24 is written on the heavenly tablets because of Cain.
b: Compare "'A curse on anyone who attacks his neighbor where no one sees!' And all the people will say, 'Amen!'" (Deuteronomy 27:24). Charles 1902 notes that "by treachery" matches the Greek dolō, the Septuagint's word for "in secret" there. Jubilees adds a curse on the witness who stays silent. Goes beyond: Deuteronomy curses the killer, not the one who saw and said nothing; compare Leviticus 5:1.

a: report all the sin that is done in heaven and on earth
p: The angels of the presence report every sin to God, even sin in heaven.
b: In Job 1:6-7 the heavenly beings present themselves before God and report on the earth, and in Zechariah 1:10-11 riders who patrol the earth report to the angel of the LORD. Charles 1902 notes the old Semitic idea, here, that sin can be committed in heaven, which the next chapter (5:1-2) shows in the Watchers. Goes beyond the Bible, but in its spirit.

a: four weeks of years
p: Four weeks of years are 28 years. Syncellus repeats the number from this book.
b: Charles 1902 quotes the Greek of Syncellus: "The first-created mourned for him four weeks of years, that is, twenty-eight years." By the book's dates, Seth is born in the fourth year of the fifth week of the third jubilee, year 130, the age Genesis 5:3 gives Adam at Seth's birth.

a: he named him Seth
p: Genesis 4:25 says Eve named him. In Jubilees the father names, as in the Samaritan text.
b: In the Hebrew of Genesis 4:25 Eve names Seth, and the site's Genesis reads "named him Seth. 'Because,' she said." Charles 1902 notes that the Samaritan Pentateuch has "he called," as Jubilees does, and that in Jubilees the father usually names the child.

a: she bore him Enoch
p: The Ge'ez spells Cain's son Unokh and Jared's son Henok. English Bibles call both Enoch.
b: Genesis has two men named Enoch: Cain's son (Genesis 4:17) and Jared's son (Genesis 5:18), who walked with God. The Ge'ez keeps them apart: Cain's son is ʾUnoḫ, Jared's son Henok (4:16). The Plain English Translation uses "Enoch" for both, as the site's Genesis does.

a: nine more sons
p: Epiphanius, a bishop of the 300s, quotes "the Little Genesis" for this number.
b: Genesis 5:4 says only that Adam had sons and daughters. Charles 1902 quotes Epiphanius (Panarion 39.6): Adam had nine other sons after these three, "as the Little Genesis contains," so that he had two daughters and twelve sons. "The Little Genesis" is an old Greek name for Jubilees.

a: Seth took his sister Azura as his wife
p: The first generations marry their sisters. From Mahalalel on they marry cousins (4:15).
b: The law later forbids marriage to a sister (Leviticus 18:9; 20:17). Jubilees lets Cain, Seth and Enosh marry sisters, then from 4:15 on the patriarchs marry daughters of their father's sister (or brother: see the variant at 4:15). Charles 1902 notes that Epiphanius (Panarion 39.7) says that once people grew many they no longer married sisters, even before the law of Moses. Goes beyond Genesis, which names none of these wives.

a: in the fourth year
p: The Ge'ez names no week here. Charles supplied "of the sixth week," which gives Seth's 105 years of Genesis 5:6.
b: The Ge'ez says only "in the fourth (year)," with no week. Charles 1902 supplied "(year of the sixth week)" from Syncellus, whose dates for these births agree with Jubilees in the tens and units. That gives year 235 from creation for Enosh's birth: Seth was born in 130 (4:7), and "Seth lived 105 years and fathered Enosh" (Genesis 5:6). The week is Charles's reckoning, not words of the Ge'ez.

a: He was the first to call on the name of the Lord
p: Jubilees reads Genesis 4:26 as the start of true worship. Many later Jewish teachers read it as the start of idolatry.
b: Compare "That was when people began to call on the LORD's name" (Genesis 4:26). Charles 1902 notes that the Septuagint, the Syriac and Josephus read it as Jubilees does, but that by Jerome's day most Jewish scholars took it to mean idolatry began then; the Targum of Onkelos says people "ceased praying," and Genesis Rabbah 23 says idols were first made in Enosh's days. Charles adds that the "began" of the Septuagint and the Vulgate implies the Hebrew huchal, and that the Targum called Pseudo-Jonathan found idolatry in the verse by taking the root chalal as "to profane."

a: Kenan
p: The Ge'ez name is Qaynan, the Greek form Kainan. Genesis 5:9 has Kenan.
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez writes the name as two words here, qay nan, and as qaynan in 4:14: the Greek form Kainan. The Plain English Translation uses "Kenan," as the site's Genesis 5:9 does. Do not confuse him with Kainam, Arpachshad's son (8:1), whom the Greek Genesis and Luke 3:36 also list.

a: Mualeleth
p: Kenan's wife bears the feminine form of the name of their son.
b: Charles 1902 explains Mualeleth (so also the Syriac list) as a feminine form of Mahalalel, "she who praises God." The son's name is spelled mäsalʾul in VanderKam's Ge'ez at this verse and mälalʾel in 4:15; the Plain English Translation uses the form of Genesis 5:12, Mahalalel.

a: he named him Jared, because in his days the angels of the Lord came down
p: Jared's name sounds like the Hebrew verb yarad, "came down." 1 Enoch makes the same pun.
b: Charles 1902 notes the play on words in the original Hebrew: Yered because in his days the angels "came down" (yaredu). 1 Enoch 6:6 says the Watchers "came down in the days of Jared."

a: They came to teach humankind and to do justice and uprightness on the earth
t: Sent to teach, not to sin
p: In 1 Enoch the Watchers come down to take wives. In Jubilees God sends them to teach justice, and they fall later.
b: In 1 Enoch 6:1-6 the Watchers desire human women and swear an oath to take them. Jubilees tells it differently: the angels are sent down for a good purpose, to teach and to do justice, and only later sin with the daughters of men (4:22; 5:1). Genesis 6:1-4 gives no motive. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels who did not keep their position. The book's version keeps God free of blame: evil comes from the angels' fall, not their sending. On how churches read Genesis 6 and the Watchers, see the "Where Christians differ" cards on 1 Enoch 1-36.

a: the Watchers
p: The Ge'ez təguhan, "the wakeful ones," is 1 Enoch's word for these angels. Daniel 4 has "a watcher, a holy one."
b: The Ge'ez təguhan renders the Greek egrēgoroi and the Aramaic 'irin, "those who stay awake." Daniel uses the singular of a good angel: "a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven" (Daniel 4:13). The site renders the word "the Watchers" in both 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

a: to learn writing, knowledge and wisdom
p: Jubilees makes Enoch the first person to write. Later Christian chronicles give the honor to Seth.
b: Charles 1902 quotes a Greek catena (a chain of comments) on Genesis 5:21: "Enoch was the first to learn letters and he wrote down the signs of heaven," and Cedrenus: "this man was the first to learn letters." He also shows that later writers such as John Malala moved Enoch's honors to Seth. 1 Enoch 12:3-4 calls Enoch "scribe of righteousness." Goes beyond the Bible: Genesis 5:21-24 says only that Enoch walked with God.

a: the signs of the sky
p: This points to the Astronomical Book of 1 Enoch (chapters 72-82).
b: Charles 1902 takes this verse and 4:21 ("the rule of the sun") as describing 1 Enoch 72-82, where the angel Uriel shows Enoch the laws of the sun, moon and stars. Like Jubilees, that book counts a year of 364 days.

a: told the Sabbaths of the years
p: Charles noted that the books of Enoch say nothing of jubilees; Jubilees gives its own system to Enoch.
b: Charles 1902 points out that neither 1 Enoch nor 2 Enoch speaks of "the weeks of the jubilees" or "the Sabbaths of the years," and calls this the writer's habit of dating back a practice he wants to commend. The angels say they made these things known to Enoch: Jubilees claims Enoch as a witness for its own calendar.

a: In a vision while he slept
p: Charles took this verse as a summary of 1 Enoch 83-90, Enoch's dream visions.
b: Charles 1902 says this verse describes 1 Enoch 83-90, two dream visions: the Flood (1 Enoch 83-84) and the history of the world told with animals as figures (1 Enoch 85-90). If he is right, Jubilees knew those chapters, which helps date it.

a: He was also with the angels of God for six jubilees of years
p: Genesis 5:22-24 says Enoch walked with God. Jubilees says he was with the angels of God.
b: Compare "Enoch walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). Jubilees reads Enoch's walk as time spent with angels. Charles 1902 notes that six jubilees are 294 years; Genesis 5:22 gives 300 years after Methuselah's birth. Goes beyond Genesis.

a: He testified to the Watchers
p: In 1 Enoch 12-16 Enoch carries God's judgment to the Watchers.
b: Compare "Enoch, scribe of righteousness, go and announce this to the Watchers of heaven" (1 Enoch 12:4). Charles 1902 says this verse assumes 1 Enoch 12-16, and that the words about uniting with women and being defiled are taken word for word from 1 Enoch 10:11. Jude 14-15 quotes Enoch's words against the ungodly.

a: we led him into the garden of Eden
p: Genesis says "God took him." Jubilees says the angels took him to Eden.
b: Genesis 5:24 says only that "God took him." Hebrews 11:5 says "Enoch was carried off, so that he did not see death." Jubilees says where: the angels led him into Eden. Charles 1902 compares 1 Enoch 70:1-3. Goes beyond Genesis.

a: writing down the judgment and condemnation of the world
p: Enoch still writes in Eden: a heavenly record of every wrong, ready for the day of judgment.
b: Charles 1902 calls Enoch here "the Scribe of God" (compare 10:17). Books of judgment appear in Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 20:12. In Jubilees the record is kept by a man, not an angel, which gives the human race its own witness against itself (4:24).

a: the evening incense of the sanctuary
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez speaks of evening incense, the incense Aaron burned at dusk.
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez has məset, "evening." Exodus 30:8 commands incense "when Aaron lights the lamps at dusk." Enoch, like Adam (3:27), acts as a priest. Charles's text and English have "the incense of the sanctuary, (even) sweet spices" (see the variant).

a: For the Lord has four places on the earth
p: Eden, the Mountain of the East, Sinai and Zion: holy places that mark the turning points of history.
b: Charles 1902 explains three of them: Eden, the first home of humankind; Sinai, where the law was given; Zion, the center of God's rule. He could not say what the Mountain of the East is. He reports Rönsch's suggestion of Lubar, the peak of Ararat where the ark landed (5:28), and also mentions that the Cave of Treasures has Seth's family living on a holy mountain near Eden. Chapter 8 returns to Eden, Sinai and Zion as the three holy places of Shem's land (8:19).

a: It will be made holy in the new creation
p: Through Zion the whole earth will be made holy, as 1:29 promised.
b: The new creation of 1:29 is centered on Zion. Isaiah 65:17-19 sets the new heavens and earth beside a rejoicing Jerusalem, and Revelation 21:1-2 shows the new Jerusalem coming down.

a: This is the one who will comfort me
p: Genesis 5:29 explains Noah's name by a verb meaning "comfort," which really sounds like another name, Menahem.
b: The site's Genesis 5:29 reads: "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the painful labor of our hands, from the ground that the LORD cursed." Charles 1902 notes that both Genesis and Jubilees tie the name Noah (Noach) to the meaning "comfort," which belongs to the name Menahem, and that he changed one letter of the Ge'ez to read "this one." VanderKam's Ge'ez reads "the one who will comfort me."

a: Betenos
p: Lamech's wife and Noah's mother. Her name also appears in a Greek manuscript of Genesis.
b: The Ge'ez name is Betenos. Charles 1902 notes that a Greek manuscript of Genesis 5:29 (Lagarde's manuscript r) gives the same name, Betenōs, and that the Syriac list has Enoshi.

a: Adam died
p: The book's dates come to year 930, the 930 years of Genesis 5:5.
b: Eighteen jubilees (882 years), six weeks (42) and six years bring the end of the nineteenth jubilee's seventh week to year 930, exactly "All of Adam's days that he lived came to 930 years" (Genesis 5:5). The book's other numbers fit around this fixed point.

a: He was the first to be buried in the earth
p: Abel had died first, but Adam is the first buried. Charles connects this to a later legend.
b: Charles 1902 says this shows that the legend found in the later Life of Adam and Eve, that Abel's body was not buried until Adam's was, already existed. Adam is buried in "the land where he was created," Elda (3:32).

a: a thousand years are one day in the testimony of the heavens
t: A thousand years as one day
p: Adam died within the "day" God warned of, because a day is a thousand years. The same reckoning appears in Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8.
b: Genesis 2:17 warns that Adam will die on the day he eats, yet he lives 930 years. Jubilees solves it with Psalm 90:4: "For a thousand years, as you see them, are like yesterday after it has gone by." 2 Peter 3:8 says "in the Lord's sight one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day." Charles 1902 notes that Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 81) uses the same argument. Shared tradition: the New Testament uses the idea for God's patience, not for Adam.

a: His house fell on him
p: Genesis does not tell Cain's death. Greek chronicles repeat this story from "the Little Genesis."
b: Charles 1902 quotes Cedrenus: "This Cain, as the Little Genesis of Moses says, dies upon his own house falling upon him; for with stones he killed his brother Abel." Syncellus says the same.

a: With the tool a man uses to kill his neighbor, with it he will be killed
p: The rule of like for like, written on the heavenly tablets as God's own way of judging.
b: Exodus 21:24 sets "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" for the courts, and Genesis 9:6 says whoever spills human blood will have his blood spilled. Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees makes the same principle God's way of governing the world, and quotes Beer that later Jewish law executed murderers by the sword rather than by their own weapon. Jesus warns that those who take the sword will die by the sword (Matthew 26:52), and Paul writes that a person reaps what he sows (Galatians 6:7). Agrees in principle; the New Testament also calls for mercy beyond the rule (Matthew 5:38-39).

a: she bore him Shem
p: Jubilees makes Shem the oldest son, reading Genesis 10:21 as "the older brother of Japheth."
b: The site's Genesis 10:21 calls Shem "the older brother of Japheth." Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees reads the Hebrew this way, as the Vulgate does, while the Masoretes and the Septuagint took it to mean Japheth was the elder. By the book's count the marriage falls in year 1205 and the births in 1207, 1209 and 1212.

a: Emzara
p: Noah's wife, unnamed in Genesis. The same name is in the Syriac list of the patriarchs' wives.
b: Charles 1902 notes that the name Emzara is also found in the Syriac list of the wives of the patriarchs and in Lagarde's Greek manuscript r. Genesis never names Noah's wife.
